```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    warning = FALSE,
    message = FALSE,
    fig.path = "figs/",
    fig.width = 7.252,
    fig.height = 4,
    comment = "#>",
    fig.retina = 3
)

library(tidyverse)
library(cbcTools)

set.seed(5678)
```

First, define the attributes and levels. These are the same as in
`design-efficiency.qmd` (and the same car survey from class 8):

```{r}
profiles <- cbc_profiles(
  price       = c(15, 20, 25),              # Price ($1,000)
  fuelEconomy = c(20, 25, 30),              # Fuel economy (mpg)
  accelTime   = c(6, 7, 8),                 # 0-60 mph acceleration time (s)
  powertrain  = c('Gasoline', 'Hybrid', 'Electric')
)
```

We need priors for two separate jobs: to find a D-efficient design, and to
simulate the choices we'll run the power analysis on. Same priors as class 8:

```{r}
priors <- cbc_priors(
  profiles,
  price       = -0.7,
  fuelEconomy = 0.1,
  accelTime   = -0.2,
  powertrain  = c('Hybrid' = 0.5, 'Electric' = -4.0)
)
```

# Random design

Make a random design (each respondent gets their own randomly sampled
questions):

```{r}
design_rand <- cbc_design(
  profiles = profiles,
  n_resp   = 500, # Number of respondents
  n_alts   = 3,   # Number of alternatives per question
  n_q      = 6    # Number of questions per respondent
)

head(design_rand)

cbc_inspect(design_rand)
```

Simulate choices according to our assumed priors:

```{r}
choices_rand <- cbc_choices(
  design = design_rand,
  priors = priors
)
```

Run the power analysis. This estimates the model repeatedly on larger and
larger subsets of the respondents, so we can see how the standard errors
shrink as sample size grows:

```{r}
power_rand <- cbc_power(
  data     = choices_rand,
  outcome  = "choice",
  obsID    = "obsID",
  n_q      = 6,
  n_breaks = 10,
  pars     = c("price", "fuelEconomy", "accelTime", "powertrain"), 
  n_cores = 1
)

power_rand
```

Note that `pars` takes the attribute names, not the dummy-coded column names -
`cbc_power()` dummy codes `powertrain` for us and reports
`powertrainHybrid` and `powertrainElectric` separately. (Leaving `pars` out
entirely does the same thing by auto-detecting every attribute.) This is
different from calling `logitr()` directly, as we did in class 8, where we had
to dummy code the data ourselves first.

Plot the results:

```{r}
plot(
  power_rand,
  type = "power"
)

plot(
  power_rand,
  type = "se"
)
```

`summary()` answers the actual question - how many respondents do we need?

```{r}
summary(power_rand)
```

Our assumed effects are large, so almost every coefficient clears 80% power at the smallest sample size we tested. That's a real answer, but it means the power curves don't tell us much. 

The `type = "se"` plot is more informative here, since standard errors keep shrinking after power has maxed out. It also means we should check a less optimistic scenario. Power analysis is only as good as the priors you feed it, so test a conservative set too:

```{r}
priors_conservative <- cbc_priors(
  profiles,
  price       = -0.1,
  fuelEconomy = 0.1,
  accelTime   = -0.1,
  powertrain  = c('Hybrid' = 0.1, 'Electric' = -0.4)
)

power_conservative <- cbc_power(
  data     = cbc_choices(design = design_rand, priors = priors_conservative),
  outcome  = "choice",
  obsID    = "obsID",
  n_q      = 6,
  n_breaks = 10,
  pars     = c("price", "fuelEconomy", "accelTime", "powertrain"), 
  n_cores = 1
)

plot(
  power_conservative,
  type = "power"
)

summary(power_conservative)
```

With smaller effects the curves actually rise, and the required sample size is much larger. When you report a sample size, report which priors it came from.

# Bayesian D-efficient design

Make a Bayesian D-efficient fractional factorial design (see
`design-efficiency.qmd` for what the tuning parameters do):

```{r}
design_modfed <- cbc_design(
  profiles = profiles,
  n_resp   = 500, # Number of respondents
  n_alts   = 3,   # Number of alternatives per question
  n_q      = 6,   # Number of questions per respondent
  priors   = priors,
  method   = 'modfed',
  n_start  = 1,
  n_blocks = 1
)

cbc_inspect(design_modfed)
```

Simulate choices on this design, using the same priors so the comparison with
the random design is fair:

```{r}
choices_modfed <- cbc_choices(
  design = design_modfed,
  priors = priors
)
```

Run the power analysis:

```{r}
power_modfed <- cbc_power(
  data     = choices_modfed,
  outcome  = "choice",
  obsID    = "obsID",
  n_q      = 6,
  n_breaks = 10,
  pars     = c("price", "fuelEconomy", "accelTime", "powertrain"), 
  n_cores = 1
)

power_modfed
```

```{r}
plot(
  power_modfed,
  type = "power"
)

plot(
  power_modfed,
  type = "se"
)
```

```{r}
summary(power_modfed)
```

# Compare designs

```{r}
plot_compare_power(
  Random = power_rand,
  Modfed = power_modfed,
  type = "power"
)

plot_compare_power(
  Random = power_rand,
  Modfed = power_modfed,
  type = "se"
)
```

The D-efficient design reaches any given level of precision with fewer respondents - the same thing the D-error comparison in `design-efficiency.qmd` told us, now expressed in the units you actually have to budget for.
